transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Stocks opened higher this morning after a big sell-off yesterday.
NPR's Scott Horsley tells us investors got a better-than-expected report on the job market.
U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs last month, far more than forecasters had expected.
A new report from the Labor Department also shows hiring in August and September was stronger
than initially reported.
The unemployment rate inched down last month, even as more than 400,000 people came off
the sidelines and started looking for work.
Wage gains?
Inched up, although probably not enough to keep pace with rising prices.
The stable job market means the Federal Reserve can focus its attention on fighting inflation.
The central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate next month.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ stock index clawed back some of the ground it lost on Thursday.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Voters plunged yesterday after investors grew fearful about the future of the AI industry.
Voters in at least 12 states this week backed new limits on AI data center development.
According to online political site Ballotpedia, voters passed nearly four dozen ballot initiatives.
NPR's Windsor Johnston has more.
Voters in Maine backed a temporary pause on large data centers.
In Wisconsin, voters demanded a say over development at a former general motor site.
One concern is who pays to power these projects.
Joshua Macy, a professor at Yale Law School, says Congress could change how those costs
are divided.
The big, big things that Congress could do are basically making data centers pay a significant
percentage of grid infrastructure costs.
But with President Trump pushing for faster development, Macy says it's unclear whether
the incoming Democratic majority can get the White House to agree to make developers pay
more for grid upgrades.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
A federal planning commission gave final approval to President Trump's proposed triumphal arch
in Washington, D.C.
That vote yesterday should have paved the way for construction to start.
But a federal judge has temporarily blocked any work, and Piers Rachel Treisman has more.
The National Capital Planning Commission voted to approve the arch on Thursday night, after
a marathon nine-hour meeting with testimony from over 100 concerned citizens.
The Trump administration said it could begin construction that same day, despite an ongoing
legal challenge by Vietnam War veterans and the governments of Virginia and D.C.
They asked District Judge Tanya Chutkin to intervene.
She did so just shy of midnight, with an order blocking construction for 14 days.
Chutkin agreed the local governments would be harmed financially and logistically as
soon as construction starts.
The administration has said that will involve 20-hour work days for two to three years.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
Pope Leo is on his way to South America, where he will travel to three countries.
That includes Peru, where he worked for more than two decades.
His 12-day trip comes after he had surgery for lung cancer last month, and Piers Kerry
Khan reports.
Pope Leo's first stop is Uruguay, Latin America's most secular country.
Only about a third of the population identifies as Catholic, less than 10 percent say they
are practicing.
Retired lawyer Ana Maria Sapurisa says that's why Uruguayans are so thankful and happy for
the Pope's visit.
This visit gives us such joy because first off he remembered us all here in this tiny
country that has so many needs.
From Uruguay, the Pope heads to Argentina, where its president's recent push to open
the country to data centers and unfettered AI regulation is sure to come up.
Pope Leo's inaugural encyclical urged ethical caution in safeguarding the human person in
the time of AI.
Kerry Khan, NPR News, Montevideo.
The weather has cleared on the border between southern Tennessee and northern Georgia, where
there was heavy flooding yesterday.
The National Weather Service says that the rain over Blue Ridge, Georgia was a one-in-1,000-year
event.
More than 10 inches of rain fell in about six hours.
Former West Virginia Democratic Senator Jay Rockefeller has died, according to member
station WETA, that is where his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller, serves as president and
CEO.
Senator Rockefeller was 89.
You're listening to NPR.

topics.text: U.S. employers add 165,000 jobs in March, far above forecasts; unemployment inches down
Voters in at least 12 states back new limits on AI data center development
Judge Tanya Chutkin temporarily blocks construction of Trump's triumphal arch in Washington
Pope Leo departs on 12-day South America trip, starting in Uruguay, then Argentina and Peru
Heavy flooding on Tennessee-Georgia border; Blue Ridge, Georgia gets one-in-1,000-year rainfall
Former West Virginia Senator Jay Rockefeller dies at age 89
